title: Stringing a story together, and saying goodbye
goal: Join short sentences into a story with the *-ka-* slot, congratulate people on special days, and say goodbye in sentences that sound like someone who has lived there.
bekal: the *-ka-* slot: "and then", linking a chain of events
holiday greetings, congratulations, and ways of saying goodbye

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kwaheri, si kwaheri ya milele
dialogs.intro: The last evening. Amina's family hosts a small dinner to send Budi off to Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.id: You leave tomorrow. We're going to miss you so much.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nami nitawakumbuka. Miezi mitatu imepita haraka mno.
lines.id: I'll miss you all too. Three months went by so fast.
lines.literal: and-I I-will-you(pl)-remember. months three they-have-passed quickly very.

lines.speaker: Juma:
lines.text: Unakumbuka siku ya kwanza? Ulisema "sielewi" mara mia!
lines.id: Remember the first day? You said "I don't understand" a hundred times!
lines.literal: you-are-remember day of first? you-past-say "I-not-understand" times hundred!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kweli kabisa! Nilifika, nikaogopa, nikanyamaza. Sasa ninaongea!
lines.id: So true! I arrived, then got scared, then went quiet. Now I'm talking!
lines.literal: truly completely! I-past-arrive, I-then-fear, I-then-quiet. now I-am-speaking!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Umejifunza haraka kwa sababu ulijaribu kila siku.
lines.id: You learned fast because you tried every day.
lines.literal: you-have-learned quickly because reason you-past-try every day.

lines.speaker: Mama:
lines.text: Chukua chakula hiki kwa safari. Na hii ni zawadi kutoka kwetu.
lines.id: Take this food for the trip. And this is a gift from us.
lines.literal: take food this for journey. and this is gift from of-us.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Asanteni sana. Sitasahau ukarimu wenu kamwe.
lines.id: Thank you all so much. I'll never forget your hospitality.
lines.literal: thanks-you(pl) very. I-not-will-forget hospitality of-you(pl) ever.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nikipata nafasi, nitarudi mwaka ujao — Mungu akipenda.
lines.id: If I get the chance, I'll come back next year — God willing.
lines.literal: I-if-get chance, I-will-return year which-comes — God if-He-likes.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Tutakusubiri. Nyumba yetu ni yako pia.
lines.id: We'll be waiting for you. Our house is your house, too.
lines.literal: we-will-you-wait. house of-us is of-you too.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kwaherini, ndugu zangu. Mnisalimie familia yote.
lines.id: Goodbye, my brothers and sisters. Give my greetings to the whole family.
lines.literal: stay-well-you(pl), siblings of-me. you(pl)-should-me-greet family all.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Safari njema! Tutaonana tena, Mungu akipenda.
lines.id: Have a safe trip! We'll meet again, God willing.
lines.literal: journey good! we-will-each-other-see again, God if-He-likes.

notes: **Mno means "too much; excessively".** Stronger than *sana*: *haraka mno* (far too fast), *ghali mno* (way too expensive). Its cousin *kupita kiasi* (to go past the measure).

**Kamwe means "not at all; never"** and is used only in negative sentences: *Sitasahau kamwe* (I'll never forget), *Hajawahi kufika* (he/she has never arrived). *Hajawahi* is another way of saying "never has".
**Asanteni is asante for several people** — the same ending *-ni* as in *karibuni* and *kwaherini*. Saying it to a whole family at once sounds far warmer than a singular *asante*.

**Nyumba yetu ni yako pia is the most characteristic East African farewell**, and it isn't a polite formula. A guest who has stayed is considered to have a place in that house forever — and if you come back ten years later, the same sentence will be said again.

**Kwaheri isn't a heavy goodbye.** For a really long parting, people add *ya kuonana* — "until we meet again". And the most common one isn't *kwaheri* at all but *tutaonana* (we'll see each other again).

grammars.title: The -ka- slot: "and then", the story-linker
body: When you narrate a chain of events, Swahili **doesn't repeat the tense slot in every sentence**. The first verb carries the time, and the rest take the **-ka-** slot, meaning "and then".
*Nilifika, **nika**ogopa, **nika**nyamaza* = I arrived, then got scared, then went quiet.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Note
rows: I went to the market, then bought bananas.
He/She woke up, bathed, then left.
He/She arrived, then found the door locked.

after: Notice that the subject prefix is still there — *ni-ka-*, *a-ka-*, *tu-ka-* — only the tense slot is replaced by *-ka-*. And the verb ending stays *-a* as usual.

This form is what makes Swahili stories flow. Compare *Nilikwenda sokoni. Nilinunua ndizi. Nilirudi nyumbani.* — three stiff sentences — with *Nilikwenda sokoni, nikanunua ndizi, nikarudi nyumbani.* The second sounds like someone telling a story.
After a command, *-ka-* means "go and…": *Nenda ukanunue mkate* (go and buy bread), *Njoo ukale* (come and eat). You'll hear this form constantly at home.

grammars.title: Linkers: from short sentences to paragraphs
body: The ten words below are what separate A1 sentences from A2 stories. Each one stands between two complete sentences, without changing anything around it.
after: Note *ili* (so that): the verb after it always takes the **-e** form from unit 14. *Nasoma ili nifaulu* (I study so that I pass), *Njoo ili tuongee* (come so that we can chat).
*Kwa sababu* and *kwa hiyo* are a cause-and-effect pair, in opposite order: *Sikuja kwa sababu niliumwa* (effect first, cause after) versus *Niliumwa, kwa hiyo sikuja* (cause first, effect after).

With these ten words, everything you've put together over twenty units can be strung into a full story. Try it now: tell about yesterday in five sentences, using *-li-* in the first and *-ka-* in the rest.

sections.title: Sherehe na salamu — greetings for special days

head: Kiswahili
When it's said
rows: Congratulations! (on a success, a graduation, a birth)
Keep it up (to someone who's working)

blocks.text: Eid al-Fitr is called *Idi el-Fitri* and Eid al-Adha *Idi el-Hajj*; both are national holidays in Tanzania and Kenya, and in Zanzibar they're celebrated on a grand scale. Other characteristic celebrations: *Siku ya Uhuru* (Independence Day, December 9 in Tanzania) and *Sikukuu ya Wafanyakazi* (Labor Day).

*Pole na kazi* is the hardest greeting to translate and the most East African: said to anyone who is working — a porter, a tailor, a teacher, a driver — and it means roughly "I see your hard work". Saying it to a stranger at work is one of the quickest ways to make that person's day better.

sections.title: Methali — ten proverbs you can already read

blocks.text: Proverbs (*methali*) are the backbone of East African speech, and they're all built from parts you already have. Read slowly; you'll recognize the slots.

head: Methali
Literal meaning
What it means
rows: Slow and steady wins the race.
little and little fills the measure
Little by little, a little becomes a lot.
if-you-don't plug the crack, you-will build a wall
A small problem left alone becomes a big one.
*Akili ni nywele, kila mtu ana zake.*
wit is hair, everyone has their own
Everyone has their own way of thinking.
come, guest, so the host may be blessed
whoever wants what's under the bed must bend down

blocks.text: Look at the fourth: *Usipoziba* is the *-sipo-* form you just learned in unit 19, and *utajenga* is the *-ta-* slot from unit 13. Look at the third: *hujaza* is the habitual *hu-* form from unit 13. You can now take apart proverbs hundreds of years old with the tables you assembled earlier.

And the last one may be the best way to close this book. *Asiyeuliza hanajifunza* — he who doesn't ask doesn't learn. Swahili speakers are patient with questions, and your first sentence needn't be perfect to be answered with a smile. *Karibu, na safari njema.*
